author: Hargreaves; Sahni; Marshall
name_in_asr: Wu-la-shi (Urasa); Hund, the ancient Udabhanda; Bilsar; Tachhasila
asr_identification: Urasa capital = Mangali on the Mangal stream (Hazara district), stupa and sangharama = Kushan basements on hill 4,219 ft S of the city; Udabhanda = Hund (Peshawar district); Bilsar (Etah district); Taxila = Sirkap
evidence: Mangali visited 9 Aug 1923: potsherd area between the Mangal stream and a nala matches the 7-8 li circuit; mound 1/2 mile SW not Buddhist; Kushan diaper basements on the hill a furlong SE taken as the stupa and monastery. Hund inspected 13 Jan 1924: Gandhara walling, diaper walls under the Muslim fort, stupa base, Sarada inscription; 20 li circuit plausible as the Indus has cut away the S side. Bilsar (Sahni): terracotta ye dharma sealing proves Buddhist monuments. Sirkap 'Mahal' (Marshall): Kharoshthi ladle naming Tachhasila
quote: the capital of Urasa must have been insignificant…These clearly defined but scanty remains may mark the sites of the stupa and songharama mentioned by Hiuen-tsang, though ghe site is rather south than south west…The 20 li which Hinen-tsang attributes to the circuit of this town seems in no way exaggerated as the Indus has undoubtedly swept away
note: Main item: Hargreaves tests the Hazara Gazetteer's identification of Xuanzang's Urasa capital with Mangali on the ground. Mizutani gives Hazara district with capital Haripur (after Watters), so the capital differs; no earlier survey view in the asr column. Hund: confirms Cunningham (ASR 02) and Mizutani (Ohind). Bilsar: Sahni's 'ye dharma' sealing gives the first Buddhist find at Bilsar, which supports Cunningham's Bilsar = Pi-lo-shan-na and Mizutani. Taxila: Marshall's ladle from the Sirkap 'Mahal' reads 'Tachhasilae' ('at Takshasila'), an inscription naming Taxila found on the site, which confirms Mizutani and Cunningham
Bengal and Assam exploration (Ekdala, Murcha-Vishnupur, Hajo); no Xiyu ji place
Epigraphy: Nalanda brick inscriptions (Pratityasamutpada texts) and the Nanaghat inscription; no location

author: Krishna Sastri
asr_identification: Allur, Nandigama taluk, Kistna district (Purvasailiya monks attested)
evidence: Brahmi inscription of c. 2nd century AD at Allur records gifts to a nikaya of the Purvasailiya sect; remains of a stupa beside the find-spot
quote: The term Purvasailiyas is interesting.and has evidently to be connected with the convent Purvasila, which with Avarasila is mentioned by Yiian Chwang in his account of To-na-kie-tse-kia (Dhanakataka)
note: Epigraphic evidence that the Purvasaila school existed in the Kistna district. It does not fix the site of the Purvasaila monastery. Mizutani puts it at the Amaravati great stupa; Allur is in the same district, c. 60 km NW, so the find is consistent with him. No earlier survey view

author: Sahni
evidence: Kara stone inscription (Samvat 1093) of Yasahpala: Sahni reads the village as Payalasa in the kingdom of Kausambi and identifies it with Paras (Pras), 5 miles NNW of Kara and c. 30 miles NNW of Kosam. With Mehayada (Meohar, 8 1/2 miles NE of Kosam) this places the kingdom around Kosam
quote: The village of Paras is just 30 miles north-north-west from Kosam…better claim to be regarded as the representative of Kausambi than Kosam…Dr. Smith’s view that Kausambi stood at or in the immediate neighbourhood of Bharhut must now be finally abandoned
note: Rejects V. A. Smith's Kausambi near Bharhut (Rewa) and upholds Cunningham's Kosam (ASR 01) with epigraphic evidence. Agrees with Mizutani (Kosam, later confirmed by G. R. Sharma's excavations)

author: Page
asr_identification: Old Rajgir: outer fortifications on the hills (Vaibhara, Sonagiri, Udayagiri, Giriak, Saligiri, Chhatagiri, Ratnagiri, Vipulagiri); Pippala stone house = tower on Vaibhara hill (Jarasandh-ki-baithak)
evidence: The traced circuit of the outer walls agrees with the 150 li (c. 25 miles) of the pilgrim. Walls stand 12 ft high E and W of the Panganga pass, with bastions and ramps. The Vaibhara tower has battered walls and small cells at the base
quote: over a distance that agrees closely with the 150 [i (approximately 25 miles) mentioned as the length of their circuit by Yuan Chwang…the tower on the Vaibhera Hill, which has been identified with the “ Pipala Stone House“ described by the pilgrims fa Hian and Yuan Chwang
note: Conservation note restating the 1905-06 report. Old city: agrees with Mizutani and Cunningham (ASR 01). Pippala: takes the Jarasandh-ki-baithak tower itself as the stone house, where Cunningham (ASR 03) put the cave behind it. Mizutani has a cave on the N face of Vaibhara, with Takakusu's suggestion that the Pippala building stood in front of it, which comes close to Page
Taxila excavations (Bhir Mound, Sirkap hoards) and Baluchistan; no location argument

author: Page
asr_identification: Kusinagara and Lumbini (Rummindei) both 'located in the Nepalese Tarai'
evidence: An aside on the eight life-scenes carved on votive stupas excavated at Nalanda
quote: from the birth in the Lumbini Garden at Rummindei to the Nirvana at Kusinagara ; both of which places have been located in the Nepalese Tarai
note: Passing remark with no argument. The Lumbini part agrees with Mizutani (Rummindei). Placing Kusinagara in the Nepalese Tarai goes against the Kasia identification (Mizutani; Cunningham ASR 01) and against the Kasia copper plate, which the department had accepted since 1910-11 (see passage 427). It probably echoes V. A. Smith's Tarai view
Rangpur rampart survey (Bengal); no Xiyu ji place

author: Krishna Sastri
evidence: Nalanda copper plate of Devapala (ed. Hirananda Shastri): five villages in the Rajagriha and Gaya vishayas granted, at the request of the Sailendra Balaputradeva, to a monastery built at Nalanda
quote: villages, four lying in the Rajagriha and one in the Gaya-vishaya (district) of the Srinagara-bhukti (division) for the upkeep of a monastery built at Nalanda—the well-known centre of Buddhist learning in Bihar
note: The plate was excavated at the Bargaon site (Monastery 1, 1921). It is epigraphic proof that the ruins are Nalanda, though this summary does not give the find-spot. Confirms Cunningham (ASR 01) and Mizutani

author: unsigned (UP conservation)
asr_identification: Nirvana stupa near Kasia, Gorakhpur district
evidence: Restoration of the Nirvana stupa and Matha Kuar chapel (1927). The copper plate deposited in the new relic chamber restates the evidence: the copper plate inscribed 'parinirvana-chaitye tamra-patta iti', found in this stupa with a silver coin of Kumaragupta (Hirananda Sastri 1910-11)
quote: ThE INSCRIPTIONS ■WHICH HAVE HELPED TO PROVE THE IDENTITY OF THESE REMAINS WITH THE PaRINIRVANA ChAITYA INCLUDE A COPPER PLATE
note: Not a new find: it repeats the 1910-11 Kasia copper-plate evidence. An editorial footnote adds that the coin dates the plate (not after c. 455), not the stupa. Supports Kasia (Cunningham ASR 01). Mizutani follows Kasia but marks it disputed, so this is the epigraphic case for it

author: Dikshit
asr_identification: Paharpur (Rajshahi district) = Somapura mahavihara of Dharmapala, one of the 'deva temples' of Pundravardhana; Nalanda, Sarnath and Kasia identified by monastic sealings
evidence: Sealings of the community of the Somapura mahavihara of Dharmapala found in the north gate area. A Gupta copper plate of 479 AD records a grant to the vihara at Vata-Gohali (= Goalbhita, in which the Paharpur mound lies) under the Nirgrantha Guhanandi
quote: The identity of the Nalanda, Sarnath and Kasia sites has been established by the discovery of sunilar sealings issued by the coimnunity of monks…It is reasonable to assume that Paharpur must have been one of the principal among the ‘ 100 Deva temples in the country of Pundravardhana ’ noticed by the Chinese traveller, Hieun Tsang
note: Paharpur is not a named Xiyu ji site. Dikshit ties it to Xuanzang's general remark on deva temples and Nirgranthas in Pundravardhana, which fits Mizutani's Rajshahi-Bogra area (capital Mahasthan). His statement that sealings fix Nalanda, Sarnath and Kasia sums up the inscriptional confirmations of Cunningham's identifications (all agreed with Mizutani; Kasia disputed in Mizutani)
Nagarjunakonda = Sriparvata (Longhurst); not a Xiyu ji place
Nagarjunakonda inscriptions; Sriparvata = Naharallabodu; not a Xiyu ji place

author: Hirananda Sastri
evidence: The Paharpur copper plate (G.E. 179) names the Ayuktaka and city council at Pundravardhana as the authorities; Dikshit equates Pundravardhana with Mahasthan
